Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
I try to erase the memory of the event
I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner, being triggered by male presence and related people is coherent, but explosion/bang sounds points toward combat, accidents, or blast-related trauma and is hard to reconcile as a core trigger here without any matching assault-context cue elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile reflects fear, avoidance, hypervigilance, fragmented memory, and negative self/world appraisals. Endorsing risky behavior pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported by other selected items; it reads as a different coping/symptom pattern than the otherwise strongly avoidant-threat profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: A marked loss of connection to community and culture is not well anchored to the rest of this intimate-partner-violence profile. The other appraisals center on danger, contamination, and shattered beliefs, but nothing else suggests cultural/community rupture, making this item feel clinically disconnected rather than tightly linked to the stated trauma formulation.

vignette: Mrs. Ellen Thompson, an 80-year-old European American social worker who is single, has been struggling with a history of physical abuse by her former romantic partner. The traumatic event profoundly shaped her daily life and psychological well-being, leading to complex PTSD symptoms that have progressively worsened over time. The abusive relationship left deep scars in Mrs. Thompson’s psyche, particularly the memory of the last incident when she was alone with him. Since then, any male presence has triggered intense fear and distress. This response is exacerbated by auditory cues such as doors opening or slamming, which remind her of those terrifying moments. The sight of known people, especially those related to her ex-partner, also evokes a visceral reaction. Mrs. Thompson’s triggers have led to several maladaptive strategies that she uses to cope with the overwhelming anxiety and grief. For instance, being alone with men has made her more vigilant about avoiding situations or times of day when nightmares might occur, such as late at night when memories often intrude on her sleep. She has come to believe that erasing the memory of the event would bring some relief, but this futile attempt only intensifies her distress and confusion. Her fragmented and distorted memories further fuel these maladaptive behaviors. When recalling the traumatic events, she can only remember them as snapshots—distinct moments frozen in time, each one a vivid picture of fear and suffering. This disjointed recollection makes it challenging for her to put together a coherent narrative of what happened. The grief associated with each memory compounds her sense of helplessness and confusion. These fragmented memories have also reinforced Mrs. Thompson’s shattered beliefs about the world. She now views the world as unsafe and unpredictable, where people cannot be trusted. This mistrust is particularly acute when she encounters men or familiar faces from her past. Her belief that she feels contaminated by what happened exacerbates her anxiety and drives her to isolate herself further. The negative appraisals have led to a cycle of heightened threat sensitivity. Mrs. Thompson’s mistrust and sense of contamination trigger her hypervigilance and constant scanning for exits in any room or building, as she remains on guard against potential threats. This hyperalert state often results in sleep problems, making it difficult for her to fall asleep or stay asleep without waking up in a panic. Over time, these behaviors have become more entrenched, creating a self-reinforcing loop where each symptom feeds into the others. The fear of male presence and familiar faces triggers her memory distortions and negative appraisals, leading to more avoidance and hypervigilance. This cycle has gradually eroded her social life and made it increasingly difficult for her to perform her duties as a social worker. Mrs. Thompson’s isolation has affected her ability to engage with clients and colleagues, often causing her to avoid situations where she might encounter men or experience triggers like the sound of doors opening or slamming. She feels that every interaction could potentially trigger a flashback or flood of memories, making it impossible for her to fully participate in her work. Her current state is marked by a deep sense of despair and fear. What frightens her most is the prospect of these feelings intensifying further, leading to complete isolation and an inability to function. Despite this, she remains hopeful that with help, she can regain some semblance of peace and control over her life. Her journey towards seeking therapy represents a critical step in breaking free from the cycle of fear and distress that has enveloped her for so long.
